name: Midnight Mutants -- TIA music player
note: A worked example of a player description. The layout was established by
reading the player at f6:$752C-$7733; audiotrace.py finds the tables, and
this says what their bytes mean.
Four levels: a song names two track pointers, a track is a list of
pattern pointers, a pattern is a count and that many notes, and a note
packs an instrument, a duration index, a waveform and a pitch into two
bytes. AUDF is five bits, so the top three of the pitch byte are the
waveform -- the chip discards them and the player reuses them.
_match: How a tool recognises that this file describes a given cartridge.
`player` is the preferred key: a fingerprint of the code that writes to
the sound chip, from `audiotrace.py --signature`. A format file describes
an *engine*, and the engine is what recurs -- this one signature covers 53
images including every hack and rebuild, which a title match misses.
`title` (substring of the header title) and `size` (ROM bytes) still work
and are checked when present. Omit the block entirely and the file is only

_banks: Track pointers in $8000-$BFFF resolve against whichever bank was mapped
when the song started, so a song is identified by (number, bank). Songs
not listed keep their tracks in the fixed bank and play the same

_note: The note's `waveform` field is an index into this, not an AUDC value.
AUDF is five bits; the player writes the whole byte and then shifts it
right by five to pick the AUDC from here. One byte, two jobs, and the
register width is what separates them.

_engine: `adsr5` is the five-stage envelope this player runs: attack, decay,
sustain, release, off. Volume is an 8-bit accumulator whose HIGH nibble
is written to the 4-bit AUDV, which is where the sub-step ramps come
from. Stage 2 (sustain) writes no volume at all -- that is why a sound
effect can leave a hole in the music.
Only ten of the sixteen bytes in a row are read.
